The post The next university crisis will not be about students using AI appeared first on HEPI.
full_text:
This blog was kindly authored by Dr Ismini Vasileiou, Associate Professor at De Montfort University.

Higher education has spent the past few years asking what artificial intelligence means for students. It is time we started asking what it means for universities as organisations. The debate has understandably focused on teaching and assessment. Can students use ChatGPT? How should its use be acknowledged? Can we still trust written assessment? What does academic integrity look like when generative AI is available to almost everyone? These remain important questions. But they are no longer the only ones universities should be asking.

AI is moving beyond the classroom and into the infrastructure of the university itself. It is increasingly supporting recruitment, marketing, student services, research, administration, cyber security, data analysis and decision-making. The risk is that universities become increasingly AI-enabled without becoming AI-resilient.

The scale of student adoption is undeniable. HEPI and Kortext’s 2026 Student Generative AI Survey found that 95% of students use AI in at least one way, while 94% use generative AI to support assessed work. Universities have responded with policies, redesigned assessment and staff development. But our field of vision risks becoming too narrow. Imagine asking a university executive team a different set of questions:

Where is AI currently being used across the institution?

Which AI systems have access to institutional data?

Which decisions are being informed by AI?

Who is accountable when an AI-supported process causes harm?

And, perhaps most importantly, would the university know quickly enough if something had gone wrong?

These are not simply questions for IT departments. They are questions of institutional governance. There is a temptation to equate AI maturity with adoption. How many staff have licences? How many pilots are underway? How many processes have been automated? Those measures tell us something about adoption. They tell us much less about whether an institution is capable of using AI responsibly.

A university could be an enthusiastic adopter while remaining organisationally immature. Staff may use AI tools with information that should never have been entered into them. AI-generated outputs may enter decision-making without meaningful verification. Procurement, cyber security, data protection, academic governance and executive leadership may each own fragments of the problem without anyone owning the whole.

The question therefore cannot simply be: How quickly are we adopting AI? It must become: How safely and intelligently are we becoming dependent upon it? That is where the idea of AI resilience matters.

An AI-resilient university is not one that resists AI. Nor is it one that creates so much governance that innovation becomes impossible. It is an institution able to adopt AI ambitiously while understanding where it is being used, what it is being trusted to do, who is accountable for it and what happens when it fails.

I would suggest five dimensions matter.

Visibility. Universities need to know where meaningful AI use and dependency exist. This is becoming harder because AI will not arrive only through explicitly branded tools. It will increasingly be embedded within software for productivity, recruitment, analytics, research, learning and administration. An institution cannot govern what it cannot see.

Accountability. When AI influences a decision, who owns the outcome? AI-enabled processes may involve IT, procurement, legal services, data protection, HR, academic quality and individual faculties. Yet if a significant decision is wrong, discriminatory or insecure, accountability cannot simply disappear into the system. Universities need clear ownership of AI-related risk and defined escalation routes.

Assurance. Universities need to move from asking whether AI can perform a task to asking when it should. Efficiency is attractive, particularly in a financially constrained sector, but plausibility should not be confused with reliability. The greater the consequence of a decision, the stronger the requirement should be for human scrutiny and verification.

Capability. AI literacy is not enough. Knowing how to prompt a system is useful; knowing when not to trust the response is more important. Staff need to recognise unreliable outputs. Managers need to understand automation risk. Researchers need to understand provenance and integrity. Leaders need enough technical understanding to challenge the assurances they are given. The goal should not simply be an AI-literate university. It should be an institution capable of exercising judgement in an AI-enabled environment.

Resilience. Finally, what happens when AI fails? What happens if a supplier changes the underlying model? If incorrect information is produced at scale? If sensitive data are exposed? If staff act on fabricated but convincing outputs? Or if AI-enabled cyber attacks target institutions whose own dependence on automation is increasing?

Universities already undertake business continuity planning for physical infrastructure, cyber incidents and critical digital services. AI dependency needs to become part of that thinking too. This is ultimately a leadership issue. One of the difficulties universities face is that AI cuts horizontally across organisations that are largely structured vertically. Teaching and learning may own one part of the conversation, IT another, research another, HR and procurement others still. The danger is not necessarily that universities have no AI governance. It is that they have fragmented AI governance.

That is why executive teams and governing bodies need enough visibility to understand where significant AI dependencies are forming and enough confidence to challenge them. The first phase of higher education’s response to generative AI was uncertainty. The second was experimentation. We are now entering a third phase: institutionalisation.

AI will gradually cease to feel like a separate technology and simply become part of how universities operate. That is precisely when the risk increases. The next stage of the debate should therefore move beyond adoption and ask whether universities can demonstrate five things: visibility, accountability, assurance, capability and resilience.

For several years, universities have worried about whether students can be trusted with AI.

The more consequential question may now be whether universities themselves can be trusted to use it responsibly. The institutions that succeed will not necessarily be those that automate fastest or purchase the most tools. They will be those that can innovate without surrendering judgement, accountability or resilience. The next stage of the AI debate in higher education should not simply be about AI adoption. It should be about AI resilience.

title: A Modest Proposal for Dual Enrollment
summary:
A Modest Proposal for Dual Enrollment Sara Brady Mon, 10/19/2026 - 03:00 AM The parent-pay model isn’t working, so how should we fund dual enrollment? Byline(s) Matt Reed A Modest Proposal for Dual Enrollment
Sara Brady Mon, 10/19/2026 - 03:00 AM

The parent-pay model isn’t working, so how should we fund dual enrollment?

Byline(s)
Matt Reed
full_text:
I’ll admit up front that this is relevant only in some states. But where it applies, it matters.

Dual-enrollment classes should be supported financially by states and/or by financial aid. The parent-pay model doesn’t work.

That position puts me out of step with some major organizations in the community college world, but I stand by it.

The idea behind financial aid is that student talent and drive don’t correlate perfectly with parental income. Making higher education accessible only to those who can afford to pay full price would leave a lot of talent on the table. And the seeming savings in terms of taxes would be illusory; if you think the nursing shortage is bad now, imagine what would happen after a decade or so of minimal new entrants. Supply and demand would work their magic, resulting in wildly higher costs for medical care.

It’s cheaper to keep producing new nurses (and dental hygienists, and teachers, and police officers, and welders, and …) than to establish bidding wars for the ever-shrinking number of incumbents. Even better, aid offers a shot at real economic mobility for students who might otherwise not have a chance. We know that full self-pay would leave out far too many and would increase inequality even more.

And yet, we apply self-pay to dual enrollment without a second thought.

Many colleges compensate by underpricing dual enrollment, but that strains institutional budgets. In budgetary terms, a colleague of mine refers to dual-enrollment credits as empty calories—they break the connection between head-count enrollment and revenue.

Some states cover the cost of dual enrollment, either through institutional support or through scholarships that cover tuition. I know that can make a difference, because we’re in the second year of a two-year grant to cover tuition for dual enrollment for students in technical majors; not surprisingly, enrollment skyrocketed as soon as the funding came through.

When I made this argument years ago at a gathering sponsored by the American Association of Community Colleges, I was informed that the association disagreed, at least as far as financial aid goes. Its position was that using financial aid for college courses in high school wouldn’t leave enough aid for when students get to college itself. (In fairness, this was shortly after the lifetime limit on Pell Grants was reduced to the equivalent of 12 semesters.)

I disagreed on multiple grounds. First, that takes the limit as given and unalterable, which it is not. Second, the entire point of aid is equalizing opportunity. When some students’ parents can afford to pay for dual enrollment and others’ can’t, we’re compounding existing inequalities.

Dan Greenstein wrote last week about the K-shaped enrollment patterns in higher education mirroring the K-shaped economy. Part of what drives the increasingly K-shaped economy is a growing sense that a rising tide doesn’t—shouldn’t, can’t—lift all boats. Instead, we take a winner-take-all economy as some sort of law of nature and set the task at hand as making sure that the few winners are as unfettered as possible. If your parents can’t afford to get you the best possible educational opportunities, well, too bad. Gotta keep the taxes down for the winners.

Doing dual enrollment the right way requires resources and rules. The resources need to be there to make the offerings sustainable, and the rules need to be there to make the offerings worthwhile. In too many states, we don’t have either. It wouldn’t take much to do this right, and to offer the students on the lower leg of the K a chance to do better. That’s supposed to be the point.

title: Connecting Dual Enrollment to Career Training
summary:
Connecting Dual Enrollment to Career Training Joshua.Bay Mon, 10/19/2026 - 03:00 AM A new Community College Research Center report identifies three ways colleges and K–12 districts can build on existing programs to help high school students earn college credit. Byline(s) Joshua Bay Connecting Dual Enrollment to Career Training
Joshua.Bay Mon, 10/19/2026 - 03:00 AM

A new Community College Research Center report identifies three ways colleges and K–12 districts can build on existing programs to help high school students earn college credit.

Byline(s)
Joshua Bay
full_text:
Dual enrollment has become an increasingly popular way for high school students to get a head start on college, but a new report from the Community College Research Center finds that opportunities to earn college credits remain underutilized, especially among students pursuing career and technical education.

The gap is substantial. According to data from the National Center for Education Statistics on 2019 high school graduates, 28 percent had taken at least one dual-enrollment course. But 33 percent completed three or more high school career and technical education credits without participating in dual enrollment. Based on the roughly 3.8 million students who graduate from high school annually, that translates to more than a million students each year missing out on opportunities to earn college credit.

The research from the center at Teachers College, Columbia University explores how colleges and K–12 districts can better connect career training with opportunities to earn college credits before high school graduation. Drawing on interviews with 135 educators and practitioners across 12 colleges, high schools and school districts, the report highlights ways institutions can strengthen these connections and help students build a foundation for continued education and future employment.

Sarah Griffin, a research associate at the center and co-author of the report, said integrating college coursework into career-focused programs can help students better understand their educational options and how further training could support their professional goals.

“When you’re introducing them to college-level coursework in the context of a program that’s already engaging their career interests, this can really help make them be aware of the fact that there is a continued path after high school … that can help lead to better jobs with stronger-paying wages,” Griffin said.

Building on existing programs: The report identifies three broad strategies for expanding career-connected dual enrollment, each aimed at incorporating college coursework and student supports into existing high school and college programs.

Griffin said the approaches demonstrate how colleges and K–12 districts can build on existing partnerships and educational structures to create more opportunities for students to earn college credits.

“The colleges and schools that we visited are not creating new programs and they’re not reinventing the wheel,” Griffin said. “They’re leveraging their existing structures or programs to create these on-ramps to students by building in dual enrollment into their programs.”

Challenges and opportunities: Griffin said efforts to expand career-connected dual enrollment face many of the same challenges as traditional dual-enrollment partnerships, including insufficient funding, uneven program quality and difficulty coordinating between colleges and K–12 districts. Addressing these barriers requires institutions to establish a shared understanding of what they want students to achieve.

“One of the key lessons that we heard repeatedly throughout the research was that partnerships need to have a shared vision for expanding college and career success for all students,” Griffin said.

“Historically, there’s been this divide between college and career, and maybe unknowingly, this has influenced the way educators work with students in guiding them towards what their options are,” she added. “But the partnerships that we visited really rejected this divide, and they really wanted to expand both college and career opportunities for students.”

Beyond strengthening partnerships, Griffin emphasized the importance of ensuring dual-enrollment courses align with students’ educational and career goals. While general education courses can help students make progress toward a degree, she said, some institutions offer disconnected courses without considering how they fit into a broader program of study.

“What we’re seeing from high-performing partnerships is that they are very carefully selecting courses that are of interest to students in order to motivate and spark their interest in different disciplines and careers,” Griffin said.

“They are clearly connecting these courses to a program of study at a community college and local four-year institutions so that students can really see the full trajectory of the courses that they’re going to take [and] what degrees they’re going to lead to,” she said.

title: Rutgers Unions Win Academic Freedom for All Unit Members
summary:
Rutgers Unions Win Academic Freedom for All Unit Members Emma Whitford Mon, 10/19/2026 - 03:00 AM Traditionally limited to full-time faculty, academic freedom protections will now extend to librarians, postdocs and clinicians at Rutgers. But without accompanying job security, adjuncts could still be vulnerable. Byline(s) Emma Whitford Rutgers Unions Win Academic Freedom for All Unit Members
Emma Whitford Mon, 10/19/2026 - 03:00 AM

Traditionally limited to full-time faculty, academic freedom protections will now extend to librarians, postdocs and clinicians at Rutgers. But without accompanying job security, adjuncts could still be vulnerable.

Byline(s)
Emma Whitford
full_text:
Rutgers University faculty unions reached a tentative agreement with university officials earlier this month to guarantee academic freedom protections to all unit members, including tenured and untenured full-time professors, part-time and adjunct faculty, librarians, clinicians, graduate student workers, and postdocs.

Todd Wolfson, president of the national American Association of University Professors, called the agreement a “monumental, historic win” at a time when faculty speech, research and curriculum have come under intense political scrutiny. Union leaders at Rutgers are encouraged by the progress, but greater job security is needed to make the protections truly enforceable for contract faculty, they said.

“International students, full-time faculty and part-time faculty in particular—we were all feeling very vulnerable,” said Hank Kalet, a journalism lecturer and vice president of the adjunct faculty union. “So these protections became a central focus for a lot of our members.”

Rutgers has two faculty unions, the Rutgers AAUP-AFT, which includes full-time faculty, clinicians, librarians, graduate student workers and postdocs, and the Rutgers Adjunct Faculty Union. Both contracts expired in June, and negotiations, which began in January, are ongoing. The academic freedom article was based on a previous clause in the Rutgers AAUP-AFT contract, as well as a separate university policy on academic freedom. Union members were happy with the Rutgers policy but wanted a version of it enshrined in the contract so that Rutgers officials could not change faculty’s academic freedom protections without unit members’ input, said Emily Marker, a history professor and member of the bargaining committee.

“We need concrete, grievable assurances that our academic freedom rights and protections will be upheld to the level that they have been in the past with this very good policy,” Marker said.

The agreed-upon article states that unit members “have the right to academic freedom, which includes the right to examine, discuss, and present ideas and perspectives when engaged in teaching, research, professional practice, clinical practice, artistic expression, professional publication, librarianship and scholarship activities, consistent with their professional judgment, without retribution."

The policy says academic freedom “means the freedom to pursue and disseminate knowledge” and “to freely discuss subjects with which unit members are competent to deal and to present and maintain their opinions and conclusions while maintaining standards of sound scholarship and competent teaching.” It also notes that “unit members, as private citizens, enjoy the same freedoms of speech and expression as any private citizen, and shall be free from institutional discipline in the exercise of these rights.”

Rutgers professors’ fears of censorship aren’t just hypothetical. Recent reports from the Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression show that attempts to sanction faculty for their speech have increased in recent years, and academics who come under attack rarely receive public support from their administrators.

A year ago, shortly after President Donald Trump signed an executive order designating antifa as a terrorist organization, Rutgers history professor and antifascist movement expert Mark Bray received so many death threats that he and his family fled to Spain. Rutgers officials backed Bray, but the situation gave the need for academic freedom protections greater urgency, union leaders said.

At nearby institutions, faculty members didn’t receive such support from their administrators; Kalet pointed to the “Fired Four” at the City University of New York—four adjunct professors who were not reappointed in the summer of 2025 after participating in pro-Palestinian demonstrations on campus. (Three have since been reappointed.)

“If we say something on social media, I believe that this [article] will protect us,” Kalet said. “If I post something … like ‘Free Palestine’ on social media, I should be protected.”

In an emailed statement, a Rutgers spokesperson said the university is “committed to supporting faculty on issues unique to higher education.”

“Since the university began negotiating with our unions in the spring, we have held 32 sessions with AAUP-AFT and 50 sessions with four staff bargaining units,” the spokesperson wrote. “We are operating from a position of fairness and fiscal responsibility while staying focused on maintaining academic excellence for our students. We will continue to negotiate in good faith, working to align union proposals with the university’s priorities and fiscal realities.”

For lecturers and other contract faculty, the academic freedom article is only the first step. Without job security that extends beyond one-year contracts, it would be difficult to make the article truly enforceable, Kalet explained.

“The biggest thing on the table for most [adjuncts] is job security,” Kalet said. “Without real job protections, adjuncts have no real academic freedom. So we won the first part of this, which is a recognition that we should have [academic freedom]. We need the second part to really hammer it home.”

title: An Uncertain Landscape for Science Funding
summary:
An Uncertain Landscape for Science Funding Elizabeth Redden Mon, 10/19/2026 - 03:00 AM New obstacles for early-career researchers could undermine U.S. innovation and competitiveness in the long term. Byline(s) Adriana Bankston Donna K. Ginther An Uncertain Landscape for Science Funding
Elizabeth Redden Mon, 10/19/2026 - 03:00 AM

New obstacles for early-career researchers could undermine U.S. innovation and competitiveness in the long term.

Byline(s)
Adriana Bankston
Donna K. Ginther
full_text:
“Can the United States Retain Its Scientific Talent?” This was the question posed by a recent panel discussion organized by the Information Technology and Innovation Foundation that the two of us participated in. The panel featured an expert discussion focused on ways to strengthen the U.S. research ecosystem, improve talent retention and ensure global leadership in research.

It was a timely conversation precipitated by the recent uncertainty surrounding federal research funding, which has led to fewer opportunities and less predictable career prospects for early-career researchers. The panel discussion, a recording of which is available to watch online, highlighted a few important themes that warrant additional discussion, including federal policy changes needed to bolster the research ecosystem, as well as to improve researcher recruitment and retention in U.S. academic laboratories in the long term.

Cuts to federal grant funding have had an acute impact on early-career scientists, who are traditionally well poised to drive research innovations in academic laboratories and to contribute to maintaining America’s edge as a global leader in scientific research. However, under current circumstances, these researchers are being recruited to other countries, leading to a significant U.S. science brain drain—which is already occurring and will continue.

The landscape for federal science funding is shifting in important ways. Focusing on two of the major federal science agencies, the National Science Foundation withheld $1.4 billion of its congressionally allocated research budget in fiscal year 2026 intended for research. This is just one of the ways in which the Trump administration is attempting to work around Congress. In contrast, the National Institutes of Health succeeded in spending its total budget in FY26, but did so in part by increasing the number of multiyear grants. While the NIH announced it had funded a record number of early-career researchers who were seeking their first grant, the shift toward multiyear grants resulted in fewer grants awarded over all.

This moment is also marked by the rise of different models of funding science, particularly at the NSF. The NSF X-Labs initiative is part of a broader funding realignment in which more federal dollars are being allocated to the NSF Technology, Innovation and Partnerships Directorate. These shifts in funding may change the trajectory of U.S. science toward more translational research. Currently, federal science agencies including NSF are having to comply with the administration’s directives for funding artificial intelligence and quantum computing, and diverting federal funds to these areas may negatively impact basic science research.

Basic science in universities is fundamental for making new discoveries and training the next generation of researchers. This type of research is serendipitous (as highlighted by the Golden Goose awards) and often generates more questions resulting from the initial line of inquiry, leading to exciting discoveries—many times by accident. There are numerous examples of impactful basic science, including the science underlying mRNA vaccines, GLP-1 weight-loss drugs and histotripsy, a cancer treatment that uses ultrasound.

Winners of the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine transformed channelrhodopsin, a protein found in a single-cell alga, into a light-controlled switch for nerve cells to better understand the brain—another example of fundamental science with important societal significance. These various examples illustrate how unexpected and valuable findings can arise from basic research projects. In that respect, fundamental research performed in universities is a public good.

We need to continue funding basic research and supporting current and future scientists in the U.S. regardless of where they come from. In this regard, recent immigration policies have also contributed to the science brain drain. For many generations, the best and brightest researchers have come from around the world to study and do research at U.S. institutions. But the cuts to research funding have led to decreases in Ph.D. admissions for international and domestic graduate students alike. In addition, the Association of American Universities recently reported a 15 percent decrease in new graduate admissions at major research universities from fall 2025 to fall 2026.

International students have also experienced unique challenges at the graduate level. These include a new rule, temporarily blocked by a federal court, that would impose fixed durations of status for graduate training, and a new proposal to levy up to $100,000 in fees for international students in STEM fields to work in the U.S. through the optional practical training program. Even before this occurred, a 2025 Nature article found that many early-career scientists from abroad were considering leaving the U.S. for research, with Europe and Canada as top destinations.

While scientists have been fighting back and speaking out against the current administration’s changing approach to science and scientists, the U.S. continues to pursue policies that create uncertainty in research career prospects and limit funding for basic science. This is a departure from the successful compact between research universities and the federal government that began with Vannevar Bush.

title: Protecting the metric, damaging the mission
summary:
Compliance experts Alex Lock and Mike Strong argue that unintended consequences linked to fulfilling BCA metrics are damaging the UK's overall mission for sustainable recruitment and quality, as set out in the International Education Strategy.

The post Protecting the metric, damaging the mission appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
There is an old principle in risk management: systems often produce exactly the outcomes they are designed to produce. The question is whether those outcomes are always the ones we ultimately want.

Student sponsor compliance is beginning to feel a little like that.

Recent changes to the Basic Compliance Assessment framework have lowered the tolerance for visa refusals and increased scrutiny of sponsors. Accountability is legitimate: universities should recruit genuine students and be responsible for their decisions.

But as institutions adapt, government needs to consider a broader question: what behaviours are these policies encouraging, and are they consistent with its own ambitions for UK international education?

The 2026 International Education Strategy sets an ambition for the UK to continue recruiting high-quality international students sustainably from a diverse range of countries.

It also presents education as an engine of economic growth, sets an ambition to grow education exports to £40 billion a year by 2030, and places international partnerships at the heart of the UK’s global engagement.

This sits uneasily alongside a compliance environment that can make caution, concentration and withdrawal entirely rational institutional responses.

This is sometimes presented as a story of winners and losers. Some institutions are already under acute pressure, while others continue to recruit strongly and grow international income, supported by established reputations and recruitment patterns weighted towards markets with lower refusal rates.

But the institutions under pressure may be an early warning for the sector, rather than an isolated group whose difficulties can safely be contained.

The distinction between institutions currently gaining and losing therefore misses the wider point. The pressures appearing first in some parts of the sector reveal how the incentives operate: as compliance risk increases, institutions are encouraged to concentrate recruitment in the same established markets, making the system as a whole less diverse and more exposed.

Universities are rational organisations. Faced with greater compliance pressure, they adapt through more screening, greater scrutiny of applications, additional credibility and financial checks, and increased caution in markets where refusal rates are harder to predict.

Sponsors are autonomous institutions and must manage their own risks; that may properly include withdrawing from a market where the exposure is judged too high. The argument is not against those individual decisions. It is that, as the metrics tighten, institutions have less scope to exercise a meaningful risk appetite even where the strategic case for developing a market remains strong.

Sponsors must retain a sufficient risk envelope to allow for appropriate innovation and the responsible development of new markets. Each decision may be prudent, but collectively they can push institutions towards the same established markets and away from the new or developing markets on which future resilience may depend.

This exposes a tension between the International Education Strategy, which calls for sustainable recruitment from a diverse range of countries, and immigration and sponsor policies that may make such diversity progressively harder to pursue.

Diversity is not an abstract virtue. It is one of the international education sector’s greatest sources of resilience. When one market slows, another can emerge. When geopolitical tensions, demographic change or economic conditions affect one country, relationships elsewhere can sustain recruitment, partnerships and influence.

The UK’s success has depended on institutions developing new opportunities and renewing recruitment pipelines rather than relying indefinitely on a handful of large markets. Those relationships also build longer-term influence through students who return home with enduring connections to the UK.

Concentration risk rarely looks like a risk until after the event. Sponsors recruiting successfully from markets currently associated with lower refusal rates may appear insulated from the pressures others are facing, but that position depends on conditions that can change.

Governments, economies, exchange rates, demographics and student preferences shift, and no major market can be assumed to remain stable indefinitely.

If a market on which many successful sponsors depend were to falter, institutions that had been pushed away from developing alternatives would have fewer places to turn. A resilient system develops future markets before existing ones plateau; a system driven predominantly by short-term risk reduction may do the opposite.

Compliance matters. It should. But so does the mission behind international education.

The concern is not that universities will break the rules. It is the cumulative effect of following them, and of responding rationally to the incentives placed before them.

If institutions reach the same conclusions about where it is safest to recruit, entering new markets becomes harder to justify and caution increasingly outweighs opportunity. Repeated over time, those choices could narrow the UK’s international reach.

These are not questions that individual institutions can resolve alone, nor is there a single sector view. Universities occupy different positions, serve different communities and face different levels of exposure.

Sector leaders can, however, ensure that the pressures already being felt, and the longer-term risks created by greater market concentration, remain visible in discussions with government. The purpose is not to argue against compliance, but to press for a fuller understanding of the combined effect of these policies.

The issue extends beyond the BCA framework. International recruitment helps institutions sustain teaching, research, employment and local economic activity at a time when domestic funding has not kept pace with costs. Policies that reduce demand, add cost or make recruitment less viable therefore have consequences beyond individual sponsor metrics.

There is a difficult policy contradiction here. International education is presented as a source of growth and global influence, yet the financial health of the institutions delivering it remains under severe pressure. At the same time, the International Education Strategy encourages diversified recruitment while the compliance framework creates incentives to concentrate activity in a smaller number of lower-risk markets.

This is not an argument for weaker compliance or lower standards. It is an argument for examining whether immigration, sponsor, funding and international education policies collectively support the ambitions of the International Education Strategy.

These tensions invite closer examination. Do the current BCA thresholds and wider sponsor policies leave institutions sufficient scope to exercise a proportionate risk appetite while recruiting sustainably from a diverse range of countries? What is the cumulative financial effect of immigration restrictions, compliance measures and additional costs on institutions and the communities that depend on them? And how might the tension between those effects and the International Education Strategy be addressed?

A policy can succeed on its own terms and still produce consequences that nobody intended. Visa refusal rates may fall. Sponsor metrics may improve. Yet the system may become less diverse, less adaptable and more financially fragile.

If that happens, the most significant consequence will not be the number of institutions that crossed a particular threshold. It will be the opportunities that were never pursued, the markets that were never developed, the partnerships that were never built, and the students who chose to study somewhere else.

Compliance matters. It should. But so does the mission behind international education, and so does the capacity of institutions to deliver it.

The question now is whether these policies strengthen both compliance and the wider mission of international education. Sector leaders have an important role in ensuring that the pressures being created now, as well as the longer-term risks of narrowing recruitment and weakening institutional resilience, remain part of the conversation with government.

title: Telangana courts international campuses for ‘Future City’
summary:
Telangana has ordered officials to draw up a policy to attract international universities to its proposed Future City development, although the University of Birmingham and University of London, both named in media reports citing state officials, have yet to confirm campus commitments.

The post Telangana courts international campuses for ‘Future City’ appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
As the southern Indian state prepares a policy to attract overseas universities, Birmingham told The PIE News it currently has no plans to establish a campus in India, while London reported no new developments beyond its August statement acknowledging discussions about opportunities in Hyderabad.

The responses come as Telangana seeks to make international education part of a wider urban and economic development program south of Hyderabad.

Known as Bharat Future City, the project is envisaged as a hub for sectors including technology, healthcare and education, alongside housing and other infrastructure.

At an October 5 review meeting, Telangana chief secretary Sanjay Jaju directed officials to formulate a comprehensive framework to attract international educational institutions, according to Indian media reports.

Officials reportedly told the meeting that London, Birmingham and four other international universities had expressed interest in establishing campuses in Future City.

The proposed policy would cover infrastructure, investment, approvals and academic programs, with Jaju also calling for consultations with prospective institutions and a clear action plan ahead of the state’s upcoming global summit.

As a global university, we regularly explore opportunities to work with partners around the world, but we currently have no plans for establishing a University of Birmingham campus in India

University of Birmingham spokesperson

The government’s stated ambition is to widen access to international-standard education, research and skills development within Telangana. Its university outreach builds on Hyderabad’s established concentration of technology, pharmaceutical and aerospace businesses.

Birmingham, however, said a campus was not currently part of its India plans. “As a global university, we regularly explore opportunities to work with partners around the world, but we currently have no plans for establishing a University of Birmingham campus in India,” a university spokesperson told The PIE.

While Birmingham’s statement does not rule out other partnerships or clarify whether earlier campus discussions took place, a July Times of India report, citing state government sources, had linked it to a possible sports-focused campus.

London’s response was more limited, referring The PIE to its existing public position. “Our position remains as set out in our August news story so there are no new developments to share at this stage,” the university said.

That August 24 announcement followed a meeting at Senate House with a Telangana delegation led by chief minister A Revanth Reddy. The university described discussions about its work in Hyderabad and opportunities to deepen collaboration in higher education, skills development and innovation.

The announcement acknowledged a growing partnership with the state but did not identify a Future City site, confirm a University Grants Commission (UGC) application or set out an opening timetable.

The initiative follows months of reported outreach, with July media reports suggesting that around 15 universities from the US, UK, Australia and New Zealand had expressed interest in establishing campuses across Telangana, particularly in and around Hyderabad.

Purdue, Northeastern, Newcastle, Chichester, Hertfordshire and Waikato were among the institutions named as exploring opportunities or holding discussions across Telangana, beyond the Future City development.

A more concrete step towards an international university presence in Telangana has come from the University of Colorado Denver, which has received a letter of intent from the UGC for a Hyderabad campus.

As previously reported, CU Denver aims to begin teaching in August 2027, subject to final regulatory approval. Business, engineering, computing and analytics would form its initial academic offering, with its location and cohort size still being determined.

Global education company Emeritus will support the campus as its strategic joint venture partner, handling non-academic functions, with admissions expected to open after final UGC approval.

The project also illustrates that a Hyderabad campus does not necessarily mean participation in Future City. Chancellor Kenneth T. Christensen said CU Denver was seeking an accessible location near employers to support industry partnerships but stopped short of linking the campus to the development.

“We are aware of Telangana’s plans related to the Future City development and look forward to learning more about these future aspirations,” he previously told The PIE.

title: Unis urged to build deeper international partnerships amid geopolitical uncertainty
summary:
Universities must invest in long-term, mutually beneficial international partnerships to maintain public trust and deliver meaningful research and economic outcomes amid geopolitical uncertainty, higher education leaders have said.

The post Unis urged to build deeper international partnerships amid geopolitical uncertainty appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
Speaking at the Times Higher Education World Academic Summit in Cape Town, leaders from Australian, European and South African universities discussed how institutions can build resilient international relationships that extend beyond memorandums of understanding (MoUs) to deliver practical benefits for students, researchers and wider society.

Glenn Toogood, industry professor of clean energy at Adelaide University, said universities had an opportunity to strengthen their standing in society by demonstrating the value of their work and building relationships beyond academia.

“Building strong relationships is something that I work on quite a lot,” he said, highlighting the potential for collaboration between Australia and France, particularly in the energy sector.

Christophe Lerouge, president of IMT Atlantique, said international cooperation was fundamental to universities and research institutes, with collaboration between the two institutions focused on areas of shared interest, including energy, the environment and information technology.

For IMT Atlantique, an institution specialising in technological education and postgraduate study, international partnerships are particularly important because students are required to study abroad.

Lerouge said the relationship with Adelaide University also reflected a shared commitment to working with industry and supporting economic development in both countries.

The panellists stressed that the success of international partnerships depended on what institutions did after signing an agreement, rather than the number of agreements they held.

“We all have MoUs with many, many universities across the globe, but what is important is what you do with [them],” Lerouge said.

He pointed to the institutions’ joint research laboratory in Adelaide, which focuses on human-machine interaction and virtual reality, as an example of collaboration that had moved beyond an agreement on paper.

The partnership also includes joint PhDs, research programs and publications, demonstrating how sustained engagement between academics can translate into tangible outcomes.

Sometimes we jump straight into partnerships without thinking: well, what is the problem we’re working on?

Glenn Toogood, Adelaide University

Toogood said institutions should begin by identifying the problems they want to solve together, rather than focusing immediately on their respective capabilities.

“Sometimes we jump straight into partnerships without thinking: well, what is the problem we’re working on?” he said.

He advocated bringing people together in person to establish trust and develop a shared understanding of research challenges, noting that different disciplines could offer valuable perspectives on complex problems.

“The real risk is that we don’t invest the time into those relationships,” he said, warning that agreements could otherwise fade away without meaningful collaboration.

Lerouge agreed that successful partnerships required commitment at multiple levels of an institution, as well as financial resources and sustained engagement.

Adelaide University’s approach also emphasised embedding relationships across institutions rather than relying on individual academics or leaders.

Lerouge argued that shared values and long-term research objectives could provide a stronger foundation for collaboration than political and commercial arrangements alone.

“What is stronger is the knowledge, the values that we share,” he said, pointing to the institutions’ common interest in training scientists and engineers and advancing work on renewable energy and climate change.

For Toogood, international partnerships also offered opportunities to strengthen Adelaide University’s position as a global university, drawing on expertise from institutions with complementary capabilities.

title: ASA expands its horizons with new campuses and TNE approval
summary:
Choosing where to study is a significant decision. Students weigh up the courses, the institution, the city and what the experience might mean for their future, says John Iveson.

The post ASA expands its horizons with new campuses and TNE approval appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
Every higher education provider in Australia has a responsibility to offer meaningful choices while ensuring that quality remains at the centre of every new opportunity.

At ASA Institute of Higher Education, that thinking has guided two important developments: our expansion into Hobart and Canberra, alongside our established Sydney campus, and TEQSA’s approval for transnational education. Together, these milestones mark an exciting new chapter in our development and create opportunities to reach students in different ways.

Our new locations in regional settings of Australia reflect a straightforward belief: students should have options that suit their individual goals and circumstances. Sydney continues to offer the energy and connections of a major international city. Hobart and Canberra provide different environments, broadening the choices available to students considering an Australian higher education experience.

Hobart offers a distinctive setting, with its regional, cultural life and close connection to Tasmania’s natural environment. Canberra, as Australia’s capital, offers proximity to national institutions and a city shaped by education, public service and innovation. Both locations bring something valuable to our growing campus community.

However, opening a campus involves much more than securing a location. It requires thoughtful preparation, capable staff and systems that support students throughout their studies. Our aim is for students across all three cities to experience a consistent commitment to academic standards, accessible support and a welcoming learning environment.

Alongside this campus expansion, TEQSA’s approval for transnational education opens the door for ASA to develop offshore education partnerships. This represents an important opportunity to extend access to Australian Higher Education through collaboration with institutions overseas.

For many students, travelling abroad for an entire qualification is difficult. Family responsibilities, employment and financial circumstances can influence whether international study is possible. TNE offers another approach, allowing education to reach students through delivery arrangements beyond the provider’s home country.

Our new campuses and TNE approval are connected by a common purpose: widening access while growing responsibly in today’s dynamic environment

For ASA, the appeal also lies in the partnerships themselves. Working with overseas institutions creates opportunities to exchange ideas and resources as well as to understand different educational contexts and develop an approach that responds to local needs while maintaining the academic expectations of an Australian qualification.

These relationships need time and care. Clear responsibilities, sound governance and effective oversight are essential. The approval is a significant achievement, but the next stage is equally important: translating that opportunity into well planned partnerships and a positive experience for students.

One TNE initiative we have been developing began through connections made at The PIE Live in 2024. Its progress has reinforced the value of sustained engagement. A conversation at an industry event can become something substantial when both parties invest in understanding each other and building a shared direction.

Our new campuses and TNE approval are connected by a common purpose: widening access while growing responsibly in today’s dynamic environment. They allow us to think beyond one city and one model of international education.

As ASA enters this next chapter, we are focused on what these developments can deliver for students and partners. Growth should create greater choice, stronger relationships and worthwhile learning opportunities. That is the ambition behind our expansion, and the measure by which we want its success to be judged in the years ahead, as each new opportunity becomes part of the student experience.

title: Building active learning: five lessons I learned
summary: The post Building active learning: five lessons I learned appeared first on Advance HE UK.
full_text:
Adijat Omowumi Inyang, Lecturer in Materials Science and Engineering Education and module organiser, shares five practical lessons from developing a Peer-Assisted Learning Toolkit for large engineering cohorts.

The conversation about active learning often focuses on why it matters. We know that involving students in discussion, collaboration and problem-solving can deepen their learning and help them develop the skills they need beyond university. Yet one question is posed far less often: how do we make active learning practical, inclusive and sustainable in practice?

This question has shaped much of my own teaching journey. Over the past few years, it has taken shape as a Structured Peer-Assisted Learning (SPAL) Toolkit, a set of ready-to-use resources I developed to embed structured peer learning directly into teaching sessions for large engineering cohorts.

In my role as an engineering educator in a transnational education (TNE) setting, I wanted my students to do more than listen to lectures. I wanted them to explain concepts to one another, challenge ideas, justify decisions and develop confidence in communicating technical knowledge. But I quickly realised there is a big difference between wanting to employ active learning and being able to do it regularly. Looking back on that journey, several lessons stand out.

Group work is not the same as collaboration

One of my earliest assumptions was that placing students into groups would naturally encourage discussion and peer learning. It didn’t.

Many of my students came from educational backgrounds where traditional teacher-led instruction was the norm. Some lacked confidence when working with classmates from different backgrounds; others were naturally reluctant to talk, question ideas or contribute in new groups. Simply asking students to ‘work together’ often resulted in one or two students completing the task while others watched.

This taught me that collaboration must be intentionally designed. Students benefit from structured opportunities to discuss, question and explain ideas, supported by clear expectations and carefully planned activities. Active learning is produced by creating learning experiences that motivate students to participate fully, not by merely seating students together.

Every student needs a reason to participate

Even well-designed group activities do not always result in equal participation. To address this, I started giving each student within the group a specific role: researcher, scribe, timekeeper, presenter, Q&A lead. These roles fostered accountability and gave each student a clear responsibility.

What surprised me most was not just the increased participation, but that students seemed to develop a stronger sense of belonging. Having a recognised role gave quieter students the confidence to contribute and made collaboration feel more inclusive, and feedback from students has been consistently positive, with learners particularly valuing the structured opportunities to participate and contribute during sessions, something that had previously felt out of reach for many of them.

Start small and build confidence

Introducing active learning does not require redesigning an entire module. Starting with manageable changes allowed both my students and me to develop confidence before gradually expanding the approach. Small, well-structured interventions within existing teaching sessions can lead to significant shifts over time.

Confidence, vocabulary and connection grow together

The more I watched these groups work, the more I noticed that confidence, vocabulary and a sense of belonging were interdependent rather than distinct outcomes. Many of my students were learning technical material in a second language, and the SPAL activities provided repeated, low-pressure opportunities to practise using that vocabulary aloud with their peers.

Explaining a concept, being questioned on it and hearing a peer put it differently all contributed to its retention. Students who might otherwise stay on the fringes of a large lecture had a reason to talk to the same peers every week, and I began to see peer learning less as a method for covering content and more as a way of building a small, functioning learning community inside a very large cohort.

Technology should support pedagogy, not drive it

Digital tools can encourage participation and increase the visibility of collaborative learning, but they are only effective when they have a clear educational purpose. Throughout this work, I found that an activity’s design mattered far more than the technology used to deliver it.

Padlet is a good example. I built activities directly around it: students responded to guided prompts, posted photos of relevant materials, commented on peers’ reasoning and built on each other’s answers in real time. In a classroom of 120 or more students, that kind of open, back-and-forth conversation simply was not possible before. The tool did not create the learning on its own, but it made the peer reasoning behind it visible in a way traditional teaching could not.

Design for transferability

The SPAL Toolkit grew from these experiences. I wanted to develop something other educators could adapt and use, not just for my own modules. Focusing on transferable pedagogical principles, rather than discipline-specific content, has enabled it to support active learning beyond its original engineering context.

That transferability has translated into real reach. The toolkit resources have been downloaded well over 500 times between April and July 2026, with interest growing steadily month on month. Colleagues within Engineering and Health Sciences Education have adopted elements of the approach in their own teaching, and the toolkit has been shared through workshops, institutional events, national and international conference presentations.

Developing the toolkit has reinforced for me that no single activity or piece of technology defines active learning. It develops from thoughtful learning design, purposeful collaboration and a readiness to reflect continuously on practice. The toolkit continues to evolve through ongoing refinement, and I hope it remains a resource that grows with the educators who use it.

For colleagues considering introducing active learning into their own teaching, my advice is simple: start with one activity, listen carefully to your students, reflect on what happens and keep refining. Educational innovation is rarely a single breakthrough; it is a process of continuous learning for educators as much as for students.

title: heise-Angebot: c’t-Webinar: KI als Schreibhelfer für Studium und Forschung
summary: Von der Recherche bis zum Feinschliff: Das Webinar klärt, wie KI-Tools beim wissenschaftlichen Schreiben unterstützen und worauf Sie achten müssen.
full_text:
Die Deadline rückt näher, das Blatt bleibt weiß, und ChatGPT liefert auf die Schnelle einen flüssig formulierten Absatz. Doch taugt der Text für eine Seminararbeit? Wer KI beim wissenschaftlichen Schreiben einsetzt, steht vor Fragen, die über bloße Textproduktion hinausgehen. Stimmen die Fakten und hält die Argumentation einer Prüfung stand? Nicht zuletzt sollte man klären, ob die eigene Hochschule den Einsatz von KI-Tools überhaupt erlaubt.

Weiterlesen nach der Anzeige

Das c’t-Webinar „Wissenschaftlich Schreiben mit KI-Unterstützung“ zeigt, wie Studierende und Hochschulangehörige KI-Werkzeuge gezielt und verantwortungsvoll nutzen. Referentin Dorothee Wiegand führt durch alle Phasen einer wissenschaftlichen Arbeit: von der ersten Idee bis zur abschließenden Qualitätskontrolle.

Viele nutzen bereits allgemeine Sprachmodelle wie ChatGPT, Claude oder Gemini, um Texte zu formulieren oder Fragen zu klären. Doch oft bleibt unklar, wie sich KI noch gewinnbringender einsetzen lässt. Das Webinar stellt daher eine Auswahl spezialisierter KI-Tools vor: Perplexity für die Recherche im Web, Consensus für die Entwicklung einer Fragestellung, Open Knowledge Maps für die Sichtung wissenschaftlicher Paper, Jenni AI für die Gliederung, ChatPDF fürs Quellenstudium und GoThesis als Begleiter von der Idee bis zum fertigen Text.

Dabei geht es nicht nur um Technik. Dorothee Wiegand beleuchtet auch juristische Fallstricke und ethische Fragen: Was erlauben Hochschulen, was gilt als redlich, und wo endet legitime Unterstützung? Das Webinar ersetzt jedoch keine rechtliche Beratung im Einzelfall. Teilnehmer lernen, die Möglichkeiten und Grenzen von KI realistisch einzuschätzen, Prompts für wissenschaftliche Zwecke präzise zu formulieren und KI-generierte Texte auf formale und inhaltliche Qualität zu prüfen. Nach dem Webinar kennen sie geeignete Werkzeuge und wissen, wie sich diese in den eigenen Schreibprozess integrieren lassen.

Nicht nur für Hochschulangehörige

Das Webinar richtet sich an Studierende, Lehrende und wissenschaftliche Mitarbeitende sowie Schüler und Lehrkräfte der gymnasialen Oberstufe. Auch Personen, die spezialisierte Textwerkzeuge kennenlernen wollen, profitieren von den Inhalten. Erste Erfahrungen mit Sprachmodellen und KI-Schreibtools helfen beim Einstieg, sind aber keine Voraussetzung.

Uhrzeit: 15:00 bis 18:00 Uhr

Preis: 69 Euro

Weiterlesen nach der Anzeige

Zur Teilnahme genügt ein aktuellen Browser. Weitere Informationen zum Webinar sowie Details zur Anmeldung liefert die Website zum Webinar.

title: L’algoritmo che decide l’università: proteste in Francia, in Italia è già tutto pronto
summary: Da settembre i liceali francesi sono in piazza, e tra i bersagli della protesta c’è Parcoursup, la piattaforma che regola l’accesso all’università smistando gli studenti con algoritmi opachi. Dietro la promessa del merito, Parcoursup amministra la scarsità di posti e risorse e riproduce la selezione di classe. E in Italia? Un Parcoursup non c’è, ma […]
full_text:
Da settembre i liceali francesi sono in piazza, e tra i bersagli della protesta c’è Parcoursup, la piattaforma che regola l’accesso all’università smistando gli studenti con algoritmi opachi. Dietro la promessa del merito, Parcoursup amministra la scarsità di posti e risorse e riproduce la selezione di classe. E in Italia? Un Parcoursup non c’è, ma gli ingredienti per costruirlo sì, a partire dal tracciamento standardizzato di tutti gli studenti, ovviamente in nome di un orientamento più “efficace” e più “equo”.

Da settembre i liceali francesi sono in piazza, e nel giro di poco si sono uniti a loro anche gli studenti universitari. La protesta è partita dalle periferie, ha raggiunto rapidamente la banlieue parigina e in pochi giorni si è estesa a tutto il Paese: oltre 1900 istituti bloccati e cortei studenteschi che hanno progressivamente intrecciato le proprie rivendicazioni con quelle di altre categorie, con il sostegno delle organizzazioni sindacali. Accanto agli studenti si sono mobilitati medici e infermieri, pompieri, agricoltori, lavoratori dei trasporti e collettivi ambientalisti, fino ai Gilet Jaunes, protagonisti della lunga stagione di lotte che ha segnato i primi anni della presidenza Macron. Il 17 ottobre quasi un milione di persone ha manifestato in ogni angolo della Francia. Una mobilitazione massiccia a cui il governo ha risposto con la “dottrina dell’ordine” e non con la politica, destinata a riorganizzarsi nelle prossime settimane, ma che ha già riportato con forza al centro del dibattito lo stato sociale, le risorse pubbliche e la dignità delle condizioni di vita. Il tutto sullo sfondo di un’opposizione concreta alle grandi questioni internazionali, a partire dall’impegno militare della Francia in Europa.

Le rivendicazioni degli studenti e l’algoritmo Parcoursup

Le rivendicazioni degli studenti nascono dalla vita di tutti i giorni in classe e parlano di dignità e di uguaglianza. Gli edifici sono inadeguati e insalubri, gelidi d’inverno e roventi d’estate. Gli insegnanti mancano, le classi sono sovraffollate e gli orari insostenibili. È una situazione peggiorata nell’ultimo decennio, sotto le politiche neoliberali della presidenza Macron (in particolare con la cosiddetta riforma Blanquer del baccalaureat “a la carte” e lo “choc des savoirs” e relativi gruppi di livello di Attal) portate avanti in nome del merito e del rigore, che nei fatti hanno significato ulteriore privatizzazione dei percorsi, più selezione e polarizzazione sociale.

Il simbolo di questa stagione di politiche ha un nome: Parcoursup. Lo abbiamo visto circolare nelle interviste, letto sui cartelli disegnati con i pennarelli dai liceali in corteo: “Nos rêves ne rentrent pas dans une case Parcoursup” (“i nostri sogni non entrano in una casella di Parcoursup”)

Parcoursup è la piattaforma nazionale che governa l’accesso al primo anno di università. In estrema sintesi, possiamo dire che se prima erano gli studenti a fornire una lista ordinata delle loro preferenze, e un algoritmo nazionale li assegnava ai corsi universitari, con Parcoursup è sostanzialmente il contrario: sono i corsi a mettere in fila gli studenti, ciascun con il proprio “algoritmo locale” e criteri spesso non trasparenti, sulla base dei voti degli insegnanti e del dossier degli ultimi due anni di scuola. La Corte dei conti francese ha chiesto di rendere pubblici questi criteri, e ha segnalato che tra i parametri usati c’era anche il liceo di provenienza.

Parcoursup è stato definito un “oracolo digitale” che si esprime attraverso una “piattaforma online per cercare di regolare l’accesso agli istituti universitari più ambiti secondo criteri meritocratici, ponderando decine di fattori, tra i quali media dei voti, attività extra-scolastiche, volontariato, cultura generale etc”.

“Un gigantesco super-io meccanico” che inghiotte informazioni e voti degli studenti e restituisce un verdetto incomprensibile, afferma il sociologo Christian Laval.

Una “piattaforma ingiusta e disfunzionale” – che solo nel 2026 ha lasciato il 18% dei candidati senza alcuna proposta di ammissione, ovviamente in numero maggiore tra gli studenti dei licei professionali – basata su una classificazione algoritmica opaca, che genera competizione e ansia tra gli studenti mentre drena risorse e tempo di lavoro degli insegnanti. Il collettivo Nos services publics ha stimato il tempo che gli insegnanti dedicano ogni anno per accompagnare gli studenti su Parcoursup pari a circa 2,6 milioni di ore di lavoro. Una cifra che vale una spesa dell’ordine di 100 milioni di euro, senza contare i costi della piattaforma e delle varie commissioni impegnate nelle università.

La sociologa Agnes Van Zanten (SciencePo) considera le piattaforme digitali di gestione degli studenti come strumenti che “perpetuano la stratificazione dell’istruzione superiore francese e il suo ruolo nella riproduzione delle disuguaglianze, introducendo al contempo nuove dimensioni più orientate al mercato [..] Parcoursup incoraggia esplicitamente i diplomati delle scuole superiori a comportarsi come partecipanti al mercato dell’istruzione e le università ad adottare programmi di reclutamento sempre più selettivi”.

Proviamo ad aggiungere due elementi di giudizio per inquadrare Parcoursup.

Due chiavi di lettura

La prima è economica. Thomas Piketty, prima in un post su X del 5 ottobre e poi in un articolo su Le Monde la riassume efficacemente: tra il 2017 e il 2026 la spesa per studente nell’istruzione superiore e nella ricerca è calata del 20%, e la scarsità di posti viene gestita da un algoritmo opaco, Parcoursup. In Italia il quadro è simile. Tra il 2014 e il 2025 il finanziamento reale dell’università statale è calato di circa il 20%, in un Paese che destina all’istruzione terziaria appena lo 0,6% del PIL, contro l’1,1% della media europea e l’1,3% di quella OCSE [si veda qui].

La seconda è politica, e discende dalla prima: se i mezzi mancano, la scarsità va amministrata. Parcoursup è la soluzione tecnocratica perfetta, una macchina che stabilisce “nel buio dei suoi calcoli” chi merita il corso desiderato, tenendo insieme due ideologie. Quella del merito: ogni studente va dove “merita”, in funzione del suo “talento”. E quella digitale-contabile: a deciderlo sono dati e modelli statistici, quindi all’apparenza in modo preciso, neutrale, addirittura “equo”. Ma ideologia del merito e funzionalità algoritmica insieme disegnano un progetto di società antidemocratico che avremmo ormai dovuto imparare a decodificare (qui e qui per un ripasso). Lo stesso della scuola neoliberale: socializzare i giovani fin da subito al principio di concorrenza e alla “vendita di sé stessi” attraverso curriculum e portfolio digitali, e affidare a tecnologie presentate come neutre decisioni politiche su cui si perde il controllo.

Per questo il problema non è la qualità dello strumento, e non basta renderlo più etico, trasparente o inclusivo. Parcoursup fa esattamente quello che deve fare: trasformare la mancanza strutturale di posti e di risorse in una questione di merito individuale, radicando nel senso comune l’idea che in tempi di scarsità l’università di massa sia un lusso che non possiamo più permetterci. In questo modo rinforza l’esclusione degli strati sociali più deboli dall’accesso a determinate carriere. Il discorso su merito, talento, orientamento, insieme alle tecnologie digitali, costruiscono un perfetto meccanismo di selezione e segregazione sociale presentato come modernizzazione.

E in Italia?

In Italia ci sentiamo più fortunati, da noi non c’è Parcoursup. Abbiamo però qualcosa che la Francia e l’Europa intera non hanno: un sistema di tracciamento standardizzato di tutti gli studenti (circa 8 milioni di test INVALSI all’anno – 2 milioni e mezzo di questionari personali), presentato come neutro (il famoso termometro) e più “equo” rispetto ai giudizi soggettivi dei docenti. È la materia prima ideale per un algoritmo di selezione.

E se nei cortei francesi gli studenti dei licei professionali scrivevano sui cartelli «On n’est pas censés choisir notre avenir à 15 ans» (“Non dovremmo scegliere il nostro futuro a 15 anni”), da noi la selezione comincia addirittura prima: in terza media, a 13 anni, quando si sceglie tra liceo, tecnico e professionale: “uno snodo cruciale nella differenziazione sociale della popolazione studentesca”.

Non stupisce allora che l’orientamento e la corrispondenza tra domanda e offerta di competenze (il mismatch) diventino un tema politico sempre più pressante, e sempre più precoce.

In quest’ottica possiamo inquadrare la lettera del ministro alle famiglie prima delle iscrizioni alla scuola secondaria, la politica dei docenti tutor per l’orientamento alle medie, la filiera 4+2, il liceo del Made in Italy, fino agli istituti tecnici e professionali diventati nominalmente licei con l’ultimo decreto scuola. La direzione è una sola: scegliere prima e scegliere “bene”, restringere l’orizzonte dei futuri possibili.

title: Big Tech, debiti e data center: cresce il rischio di una crisi AI
summary:
Le Borse hanno ridimensionato le maggiori imprese tecnologiche dopo gli allarmi su memorie, neocloud e data center. Valutazioni elevate, tassi in crescita e ricorso al debito rendono gli investimenti nell’AI e i mercati finanziari sempre più dipendenti dalla stessa scommessa globale

L'articolo Big Tech, debiti e data center: cresce il rischio di una crisi AI proviene da Agenda Digitale.
full_text:
“There’s a new story in stock markets: If you aren’t touched by AI, good luck. AI is sucking in capital and squeezing the rest of the market, where stocks face higher interest rates and oil prices without a sexy technology story to sell (C’è una nuova storia sui mercati azionari: se l’AI non ti tocca, buona fortuna. L’AI sta assorbendo capitali e spremendo il resto del mercato, dove i titoli si trovano ad affrontare tassi di interesse e prezzi del petrolio più elevati, senza una storia tecnologica affascinante da vendere)” scriveva The Wall Street Journal (WSJ) in un articolo poco profetico, almeno nelle sue previsioni sul breve periodo.

Dieci giorni dopo la musica è cambiata, per una sequenza di notizie – apparentemente non così rilevanti – che hanno però messo in luce il grande nervosismo del mercato sulle valutazioni così alte delle imprese tech e sul crescente ricorso al debito per finanziare gli investimenti di molte di esse (soprattutto di quelle operanti nella filiera dei semiconduttori destinati agli AI data center), in una fase di forte crescita dei tassi di interesse statunitensi.

Investimenti AI e mercati finanziari: l’allarme arriva dalle borse

L’annuncio della cinese CXMT di un breaktrhough che avrebbe permesso una riduzione dei costi delle memorie – il settore in cui essa opera con una capitalizzazione prossima al mezzo trilione (ovvero 500 miliardi) di dollari – ha colpito duramente i valori di Borsa delle due imprese sudcoreane Samsung e SK Hynix (che da sole pesano per circa la metà dell’indice di Borsa KOSPI del Paese) e della statunitense Micron, che insieme dominano il mercato mondiale: Micron ha perso il 15,8% nelle sette giornate di Borsa fra il 6 e il 16 novembre, Samsung il 20,2% e SK Hynix il 24,1%.

Più o meno negli stessi giorni un allarme è arrivato dall’Australia (ben descritto in “The data centre IPO debacle that sparked a market meltdown: Decisions by Australian groups Firmus and AirTrunk have added to concerns about the AI borrowing frenzy”, FT, 16 ottobre), sull’eccessivo ricorso all’indebitamento delle cosiddette neocloud: Firmus, una neocloud con Nvidia e Blackstone alle sue spalle, ha rinunciato – per le condizioni di mercato non favorevoli – ad effettuare un IPO pianificato da tempo, che avrebbe dovuto essere il secondo in assoluto per dimensioni nella storia australiana e che le avrebbe attribuito un valore di 30 miliardi di $, e poco dopo è stata la volta di AirTrunk, un’altra neocloud australiana, di rinunciare all’IPO alla Borsa di Singapore.

La statunitense CoreWeave, la pioniera fra le neocloud fatte nascere da Nvidia, è stata quella che più risentito di questi annunci: i suoi bond sono caduti nella categoria dei cosiddetti “distressed” (con un elevato rischio cioè di non essere rimborsati alla scadenza) e la sua capitalizzazione è scesa del 25% rispetto a inizio mese.

La febbre si è poi estesa alle altre tech, come si può vedere dalla Tab. 1 che mette a confronto le capitalizzazioni del 6 e del 16 novembre delle 12 top tech a livello mondiale (nella quasi totalità statunitensi con le sole eccezioni della taiwanese TSMC e della sudcoreana Samsung): tutte in caduta più o meno pronunciata, con l’eccezione di Microsoft e soprattutto di Apple, che è tornata a superare la soglia dei 5 trilioni di $, riducendo la distanza da Nvidia che viceversa ha perso oltre il 10% nello stesso intervallo di tempo.

Big Tech e mercati finanziari: il peso della filiera AI

Nonostante la caduta le imprese tech – quasi tutte presenti (anche se con pesi e ruoli diversi) nella filiera dell’AI – mantengono una posizione dominante nell’ambito delle imprese quotate a livello sia statunitense sia globale.

Il punto interrogativo è mio, il testo è una libera traduzione del sottotitolo – “The tremor seen this week could be a foretaste of things to come” dell’Opinion di Richard Waters del 15 ottobre su FT “Risk of an AI crunch for stock markets is rising”: una tesi non nuova dell’autore, che sembra esprimere una sua forte convinzione che il rischio di una “AI crunch” sul mercato azionario stia crescendo, che i tremori visti questa settimana possano far presagire sempre più un terremoto.

Le fosche previsioni di Waters poggiano sulla constatazione che (Fig. 4) il capex complessivo delle hyperscalers (le 4 cui il titolo è spesso riservato più Oracle) raggiungerà a fine anno gli 800 miliardi di dollari – poco meno di un terzo del PIL previsto per l’Italia dall’IMF per il 2026 di 2552 miliardi di dollari – e supererà per la prima volta il loro cash flow operativo.

Sulla constatazione che per remunerare “decentemente” questi investimenti gli acquisti di servizi AI prodotti da questi data center dovrebbero ammontare nel 2032 (secondo le stime della Brookings Institution) a oltre il 9% del PIL statunitense.

Sulla constatazione che l’attuale prevalenza della domanda di servizi forniti dagli AI data center rispetto alla capacità di offerta disponibili potrebbe cambiare di segno, dati i lunghi tempi che intercorrono fra il momento della spesa e quello dell’entrata in funzione dei .centri stessi.

“L’hype nei riguardi delle nuove tecnologie è una tentazione umana inevitabile, e talvolta è pagante, ma occorre ricordare che alla fine gli investitori vogliono ritorni sui soldi messi in gioco”.

È la libera traduzione dell’incipit di una Opinion dell’Editorial Board di WSJ pubblicata il 15 ottobre – “The Market’s Rude Reminder on AI: Sooner or later investors will demand returns, and there will be losers”, che sostiene che sia troppo presto per interpretare la caduta dei prezzi della settimana come una correzione del mercato nei riguardi dell’AI, ma che non possa essere ignorata come un severo avvertimento.
